content: 1. Preventative maintenance involves having trained personnel available on-site to repair and troubleshoot equipment issues effectively. 2. Consumables used in pathology laboratories include standard medical products, specialized shelf-stable products, and finite-use products. Bulk purchasing of standard products and recycling of bulk reagents such as formalin, xylene, and alcohol are also essential practices. 3. National or regional pricing schemes can help standardize costs, while warehousing with rolling stock supply ensures consistent availability of materials. 4. Laboratory services should be organized in a tiered system to optimize efficiency and resource allocation. 5. General overheads for laboratory operations include electricity, water supply, facility administration, laboratory cleanliness, and waste management. Renewable energy sources like solar power and rooftop water reservoirs, along with on-site water treatment facilities, can enhance sustainability. National or regional waste disposal plans should also be implemented. 6. Revenue from public sector funds can be sourced through direct government funding, continuous cost reviews, and active multi-year recruitment of funds with transparent reporting. 7. Revenue from third parties, including patients, may involve direct donor funding, social insurance schemes, out-of-pocket costs, tiered systems based on income, mutual benefit programs, installment payments, and value-based pricing informed by health technology assessments. Equity in service provision must be maintained, ensuring all patients receive the same quality of care regardless of funding source. 8. Pathology laboratory results directly impact patient treatment and health outcomes, necessitating the highest level of accuracy. A quality management system must be established to coordinate and control activities related to quality. 9. The quality management system should address 12 essential components, including facilities and safety, equipment, purchasing and inventory, personnel, process control, information management, and occurrence management, among others. 10. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) are critical documents that provide step-by-step instructions for laboratory procedures. Each SOP should include the test title, purpose, and detailed instructions, and must be regularly updated. 11. Quality control in histopathology and cytopathology requires careful monitoring of reagents, solutions, and equipment. Proper labeling, storage, and daily checks of stains and reagents are necessary to ensure consistent results. 12. An information management system is essential for managing patient data effectively. This system can be paper-based, partially computerized, or fully computerized, and should support timely reporting and decision-making. 13. Accurate disease coding, such as using the WHO International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) and the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology (ICD-O), is vital for tracking disease patterns and informing cancer control strategies. 14. Occurrence management involves identifying and addressing errors or near-errors in laboratory processes. This includes pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases, with measures like clinician education, secondary checks, and barcoding to minimize errors. 15. Assessment of laboratory quality management systems ensures compliance with regulatory, accreditation, and customer requirements. External quality assessment (EQA) programs, such as proficiency testing and rechecking, are critical for maintaining professional standards. 16. Accreditation of pathology laboratories involves formal recognition of their competence to perform specific tasks according to established standards. This includes process control, document control, personnel management, and compliance with health and safety measures. 17. Process improvement focuses on continuous enhancement of laboratory quality over time. Defining and tracking quality indicators ensures transparency and accountability for results. 18. Internal and external audits provide valuable insights into laboratory performance, identifying areas for corrective action and process improvement. Internal audits increase staff awareness and prepare laboratories for external evaluations. 19. Laboratories must maintain comprehensive records of all activities, including specimen handling, equipment maintenance, quality control data, and audit results, to ensure traceability and accountability. 20. Effective management of facilities, equipment, reagents, and data is essential for the smooth operation of pathology laboratories. This includes proper specimen collection, transportation, and examination procedures, as well as clear reporting of results.
